title: Hierarchical fragmentation–aware KV block allocator with eviction-quantiles and soft-prefetch throttling
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Summary:
Design, implement, and validate a hierarchical block allocator for the KV cache that is fragmentation-aware and integrates eviction quantiles and a soft-prefetch throttle to reduce GPU OOMs and tail latency under mixed-length continuous batching workloads. This ticket covers design docs, a prototype allocator in the runtime, microbenchmarks, and an initial canary rollout on a dedicated pool.

Background & motivation:
We've seen persistent tail OOM and throughput drops when request distributions include many long sequences interleaved with short ones. Existing slab + paged approaches lead to internal fragmentation and suboptimal eviction choices when blocks are allocated at single-grain sizes. Prefetch heuristics that aggressively pull KV pages from host/GPU also cause thermal pressure and PCIe contention on oversubscribed nodes. To keep latency SLOs while minimizing token cost, we need a more nuanced allocator that: 1) tracks fragmentation at multiple size classes; 2) uses eviction quantiles (not just LRU) to avoid evicting recently accessed long-context shards; and 3) exposes a throttle that softly limits prefetch work when thermal/PCI metrics exceed thresholds.

Design goals & acceptance criteria:
- Reduce 95th/99th tail latency for mixed-length batches by >= 15% in canary workloads compared to current slab allocator.
- Reduce token-level OOMs under pathologically mixed workloads by >= 50%.
- No regressions (>2%) in median throughput for short-only production traffic.
- Prefetch throttle must be tunable per-pool and adaptive to thermal/PCI counters.

High-level design:
1) Hierarchical fragmentation accounting: maintain compact per-block-size histograms (power-of-two classes from 512B -> 1MB) that estimate free/used fragmentation. When allocating, prefer fitting the smallest class whose slack is under-utilized to reduce leftovers.
2) Block meta with hotness quantiles: for each KV slice we persist a small hotness sketch (decayed counter + sample timestamps). Eviction decisions are based on quantile buckets (e.g., bottom 25% cold, 25–75% warm, top 25% hot) rather than pure LRU to avoid thrashing long-context caches during bursts.
3) Soft-prefetch throttle: central controller monitors GPU temperature, host-to-device PCIe bandwidth saturation, and prefetch queue depth. When thresholds are crossed, the controller reduces prefetch rate and converts some prefetches to on-demand pulls with tight deadlines.
4) Shadow host staging + RDMA-friendly fallbacks: introduce a bounded host-staging ring for prefetched pages; when the ring is saturated, we opportunistically compress older pages and fall back to an RDMA-friendly transfer path where available.
5) WAL-friendly write batching: when evicting dirty metadata (for private deployments with persisted KV), batch writes to reduce IOPS and lock contention.

Implementation plan (incremental):
- Phase 1 (prototype): add hierarchical accounting & basic block allocator; metrics + debug traces. (ENG-87102-A)
- Phase 2 (eviction quantiles): implement hotness sketch and quantile-driven eviction policy; unit tests + local sim harness. (ENG-87102-B)
- Phase 3 (soft-prefetch): implement prefetch controller tied to thermal and PCI counters; integrate host-staging ring. Add knobs and circuit-breaker. (ENG-87102-C)
- Phase 4 (canary & telemetry): deploy to a small dedicated pool, collect dashboards (latency tails, OOMs, prefetch hit rate, PCI usage), iterate. (ENG-87102-D)

Trade-offs considered:
- Complexity vs determinism: quantile-based eviction is less deterministic than LRU but avoids pathological thrash. We'll add a deterministic tie-breaker using last-accessed-epoch to aid debugging.
- Memory overhead: hotness sketches add ~8–24 bytes per slice; hierarchical histograms add modest global state per allocator. We accept this for improved allocation quality.
- Prefetch latency vs thermal safety: soft-prefetch may increase cold miss latency during sustained high PCI/thermal pressure. To limit user impact, we convert some prefetches to prioritized on-demand fetches with deadlines for active requests.

Telemetry & observability:
- New metrics: alloc_fragmentation_by_class, eviction_quantile_counts, prefetch_rate_controller_state, host_staging_fill, prefetch_missed_deadlines.
- Dashboards: per-pool fragmentation heatmap, prefetch controller state timelines, PCIe saturation vs prefetch rate.
- Logging: structured traces on eviction decisions, including quantile and last_access_epoch, to aid postmortem.

Acceptance tests & benchmarks:
- Local sim harness: build synthetic workload mixing 5% long (8k+ tokens), 70% short (<256 tokens), 25% medium. Run with different batch concurrency and GPU oversubscription to measure tail latency and OOMs.
- Microbench: measure allocation latency per-request under high concurrency.
- Canary experiment: route 1–2% of production-like traffic in dedicated runtime-1.20 pool and compare to control for 48h.

Rollout plan:
- Stage 1: internal runtime QA on a dev pool (2 days)
- Stage 2: canary to dedicated pool with lower-cost models (1 week)
- Stage 3: expanded canary to mixed models and limited hosted lanes (2 weeks)
- Stage 4: full rollout with runtime-1.20 opt-in flag across Dedicated clusters (gradual)

Open questions / risks:
- How to persist hotness sketches across restarts for private/on-prem deployments (we may accept cold restart decay).
- Interactions with existing KV sharding: quantiles must be globally meaningful across shards; we may need a lightweight cross-shard sampler for fairness.
- Security: ensure metadata for hotness sketches does not expose request/user-sensitive patterns (likely low risk but flagged).

Next steps (short):
- Finalize proto API by 2025-01-20 (Diego + runtime infra).
- Implement Phase 1 prototype by 2025-01-31.
- Attach sim harness script and config examples to this ticket.
